text: A Turkic dynasty from Ghazni whose sultan Mahmud raided deep into India and whose court fostered Persian literature, including Ferdowsi's Shahnameh.

Kazakh armies were tribal cavalry led by sultans and by renowned warriors (batyr), fighting with bows, lances and sabres and, from the seventeenth century, increasingly with matchlocks. Under Qasim Khan (r. c. 1511–1521) they were feared across Central Asia, and Muhammad Haidar Dughlat credits him with a following of about a million people. The khans fought the Shaybanids of Bukhara for the towns of the Syr Darya, the Nogais to the west and the Moghuls and Oirats to the east. Haqnazar Khan (r. c. 1538–1580) restored Kazakh power after a period of defeats, and Tauekel Khan seized Tashkent, Turkistan and other towns from Bukhara in 1598, gains held under his successor Esim Khan. From the 1630s the main threat came from the Dzungar Khanate. In 1643 Jahangir Khan, with a small force of musketeers and help from Yalangtush Bahadur of Samarkand, is said to have checked the Dzungar ruler Erdeni Batur at the Battle of Orbulaq in the mountains of Zhetysu. Dzungar pressure grew under Galdan and Tsewang Rabtan and culminated in the invasion of 1723. The three juzes then joined forces under Abulkhair Khan and batyrs such as Kabanbai and Bogenbai, winning victories at Bulanty around 1727–1728 and at Anyrakai around 1729–1730, but their alliance broke apart soon afterwards over rivalry for leadership.

The Dzungar Khanate was the last great independent nomadic empire of Inner Asia, and its contest with the Qing decided the political map of Central Eurasia. To defeat it the Kangxi, Yongzheng and Qianlong emperors built supply lines, granaries and military colonies deep into the steppe. The Dzungar wars drew the Qing into absorbing Khalkha Mongolia, whose princes submitted at the Dolon Nor assembly in 1691, into establishing a protectorate over Tibet after 1720, and finally into conquering Dzungaria and the Tarim Basin, which became Xinjiang, the 'new frontier'. At the same time Dzungar pressure pushed the Kazakh juzes into dependence on Russia, and the Russian and Qing empires later divided Central Asia across the lands left open by the Dzungars' fall. The khanate's patronage of Buddhism and Zaya Pandita's Clear Script left a lasting mark on Oirat and Kalmyk culture, and the script remained in use among Kalmyks and Oirats into the twentieth century. The Dzungars are remembered very differently in different countries: as a menace in Kazakh history, as rebels in official Qing histories, and often as heroic defenders of Mongol independence in Mongolia. Their destruction is also one of the clearest cases of mass killing in early modern Asia, and many modern historians describe it as a genocide.

The Republic of China was one of the earliest republics in Asia, and its founding ended the imperial system that had governed China since 221 BCE. Its symbols and institutions, from the ‘Double Tenth’ national day to the five-branch constitution, carried Sun Yat-sen’s blend of Western republicanism and Chinese tradition, and Sun is honoured as ‘Father of the Nation’ in Taiwan and as a forerunner of the revolution in the People’s Republic of China. The Nationalist government ended most foreign privileges in China: the United States and Britain gave up extraterritoriality in 1943, and at the Cairo Conference that year Chiang Kai-shek met Franklin D. Roosevelt and Winston Churchill as an Allied leader. In 1945 the Republic became a founding member of the United Nations and one of the five permanent members of its Security Council. On Taiwan it became one of the ‘Four Asian Tigers’, and the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, founded in 1987, grew into the world’s largest contract chipmaker, placing the island at the heart of global technology supply chains. Its democratisation showed that a Chinese-speaking society could sustain competitive elections and a free press, and in 2019 it became the first place in Asia to legalise same-sex marriage. The question of its status remains among the most sensitive in international politics.
Egypt as the richest province of the Roman and Byzantine empires, the granary of Rome and a cradle of Christian monasticism.

The Funj Sultanate, known from its capital as the Sultanate of Sennar, arose on the Blue Nile at the beginning of the sixteenth century. The origins of the Funj themselves are uncertain: they appear in the sources as a cattle-keeping people of the southern Gezira and the upper Blue Nile, and theories linking them to the Shilluk, to Bornu or to Umayyad refugees from Arabia remain unproven, the last being a later genealogy that bolstered the dynasty’s Muslim credentials. According to the Funj Chronicle and later tradition, their leader Amara Dunqas founded Sennar in 1504, a date accepted by most historians though it rests on late sources. Around the same time, the Christian Nubian kingdom of Alodia, long in decline, collapsed. Its capital Soba, near the confluence of the Blue and White Niles, was destroyed by an alliance of the Funj and the Arab tribes of the Qawasma led by Abdallah Jamma, whose descendants, the Abdallab, ruled the northern part of the kingdom from Qerri as vassals of Sennar. The exact sequence of these events and the date of Soba’s fall are debated. By the middle of the sixteenth century the Funj had accepted Islam, and their sultans ruled over the Gezira between the two Niles and, through the Abdallab, over the Nile valley northward towards the Third Cataract.

Morocco under the Saadis remained a largely rural society of farmers and pastoralists, organised in Arab and Berber tribes, with Fez and Marrakesh as its great cities. Religious authority was widely shared with Sufi brotherhoods and saintly lineages, whose lodges, or zawiyas, were centres of learning, charity and local power; the Saadis themselves owed their rise to this world. The most dynamic part of the economy was the production of cane sugar in the Sus and around Marrakesh, in large mills and estates under royal control, and sugar was exported to England, the Netherlands and Italy. Moroccan saltpetre, needed for gunpowder, was traded for English cloth and weapons. After the conquest of Songhai in 1591, gold from the Niger valley arrived in Marrakesh, earning Ahmad al-Mansur the name al-Dhahabi, the Golden, though the flow fell short of his hopes within a few years. Jewish communities played a major role in trade and finance, and the arrival of Muslims and Moriscos expelled from Spain, culminating in the expulsions of 1609–1614, brought craftsmen, soldiers and corsairs to the Moroccan towns. Plague struck repeatedly, notably in the epidemic of the late 1590s and early 1600s that killed al-Mansur himself.

The prosperity of Miletus rested on commerce, manufacture and colonisation. Milesian wool and woollen cloth were prized across the Greek world, and the city's merchants traded with Lydia and the Anatolian interior, with Egypt and with the Black Sea. Pliny the Elder credited Miletus with founding some ninety colonies, a figure that is probably exaggerated but reflects a real and sustained movement. Milesians settled the shores of the Hellespont, the Propontis and the Black Sea, founding Abydos, Cyzicus, Sinope, Histria, Apollonia Pontica, Olbia and Panticapaeum, and these colonies sent grain, fish, timber and slaves in return for wine, oil and manufactured goods. In Egypt, Milesians were among the Greeks trading at Naucratis, where they had their own sanctuary of Apollo. Some of the earliest coins, small pieces of electrum stamped with a lion, may have been struck at Miletus in the late seventh or early sixth century BCE. Society was sharply divided between wealthy landowners and merchants and a large population of craftsmen and labourers; according to Plutarch, factions called the Ploutis, the party of the rich, and the Cheiromacha, the party of those who worked with their hands, fought bitterly for control. Religious life centred on Apollo, worshipped at Didyma and in the city as Apollo Delphinios, whose guild of singers, the Molpoi, stood at the heart of civic cult.

Samos left a lasting mark through its engineering, its sanctuary and the people it produced. Herodotus singled out three Samian works as the greatest in the Greek world: the harbour mole, the temple of Hera, which he considered the largest temple he knew, and the tunnel built by the engineer Eupalinos of Megara to bring water to the city. The tunnel, 1,036 metres long, was dug through a mountain from both ends at once, and the two teams met with only a small error, a remarkable feat of surveying that can still be walked through today. The town of Pythagoreio and the Heraion are now together a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Samos was the birthplace of Pythagoras, who left for Croton in southern Italy, by tradition to escape the rule of Polycrates, and whose followers shaped Greek mathematics and philosophy. The Eleatic philosopher Melissus was a Samian statesman, the historian Duris came from the island, and Epicurus was born there to an Athenian settler family in 341 BCE. Aristarchus of Samos, working in the third century BCE, proposed that the earth moves around the sun, an idea that anticipated Copernicus by some eighteen centuries. The Samian expedition of Colaeus to Tartessos also became one of the best-known stories of early Greek long-distance trade.
City-state of Attica that created democracy, led the Delian League and produced the drama, philosophy and architecture at the heart of Classical Greek culture.

Delphi was the nearest thing the Greek world had to a common religious centre. Its oracle advised on colonies, laws, cults, wars and private dilemmas, and its famous responses, whatever their authenticity, shaped how Greeks told their history. Herodotus records that Croesus was told he would destroy a great empire if he attacked Persia, and that the Athenians in 480 BCE were told to trust in their wooden walls, which Themistocles read as their fleet. In Plato's Apology Socrates traces his philosophical mission to the Pythia's answer that no one was wiser than he. Maxims inscribed at the temple, such as Know yourself and Nothing in excess, became touchstones of Greek ethics. The Pythian Games, reorganised as a panhellenic festival in 586 or 582 BCE, ranked second only to the Olympic Games and gave music a special place. Dedications made Delphi a showcase of Greek art and politics: the Athenian Treasury, the bronze Charioteer of Delphi of about 475 BCE, and the Serpent Column set up after the Battle of Plataea in 479 BCE, which Constantine the Great later moved to Constantinople, where its remains still stand in the old Hippodrome of Istanbul. Two Delphic hymns to Apollo of the late second century BCE, carved with musical notation, are among the most important survivals of ancient Greek music. French excavations from 1892 uncovered the site.

The Celtiberian economy rested on stock-raising and cereal farming on the cold, high plateau. Sheep, cattle and horses were the main wealth, and Diodorus Siculus describes Celtiberians wearing rough black woollen cloaks. Iron was mined in the Moncayo range and around Bilbilis and Turiaso, and Celtiberian smiths were renowned: Diodorus says they buried iron plates until the weaker parts rusted away and forged weapons from what remained. Society was dominated by warrior elites bound to followers by clientage, and some followers were said to pledge their lives to a leader in a bond modern scholars call the devotio iberica. Agreements between individuals and communities were sealed by pacts of hospitality, recorded on small bronze tokens, the tesserae hospitales, often shaped as animals or clasped hands. Religion is known from inscriptions and classical reports; the rock inscriptions of Peñalba de Villastar name the god Lugus, also worshipped by Celts elsewhere in Europe, and Silius Italicus and Aelian report that warriors killed in battle were left to be eaten by vultures, believed to carry them to the heavens. In the second and first centuries BCE the Celtiberians adapted the Iberian script to write their own language, as on the bronze tablets from Botorrita, the ancient Contrebia Belaisca, and many towns minted silver denarii and bronze coins bearing a horseman, used largely to pay for Roman taxes and troops.

Conquest strained the Republic’s institutions. In 133 BCE the tribune Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus proposed to redistribute public land to poor citizens and was killed by senators; his brother Gaius met the same fate in 121 BCE. The Social War of 91–88 BCE forced Rome to grant citizenship to the Italian allies, and in 88 BCE Lucius Cornelius Sulla marched his army on Rome, beginning civil wars that ended with his dictatorship and the proscriptions of 82–81 BCE. Extraordinary commands made Gnaeus Pompeius Magnus master of the East, where he defeated Mithridates VI. In 60 BCE Pompey, Marcus Licinius Crassus and Julius Caesar formed an informal alliance known as the First Triumvirate, but after Crassus died at Carrhae in 53 BCE Caesar and Pompey fell out. Caesar crossed the Rubicon in 49 BCE, defeated Pompey at Pharsalus in 48 BCE and was made dictator for life early in 44 BCE, before senators led by Brutus and Cassius murdered him on the Ides of March. The Second Triumvirate of Mark Antony, Octavian and Lepidus defeated the assassins at Philippi in 42 BCE. Octavian defeated Antony and Cleopatra VII at Actium in 31 BCE and annexed Egypt in 30 BCE. In January 27 BCE he formally restored the Republic to the Senate and people and received the name Augustus, keeping real power and founding the Principate.

The league's army was a citizen militia drawn from the member cities, supplemented by mercenaries paid from federal funds, with a cavalry force under a federal hipparch and a small fleet under a navarch. Under Aratus it was weak in pitched battle: he excelled at night attacks and surprises such as the capture of Acrocorinth, but the league suffered a series of defeats at the hands of Cleomenes III, at Mount Lykaion, Ladokeia and the Hekatombaion near Dyme in 227–226 BCE, which forced Aratus to call in Antigonus III Doson of Macedon. The army was transformed by Philopoemen of Megalopolis, who as hipparch and then, from 208 BCE, as general retrained the cavalry, re-equipped the infantry as a Macedonian-style phalanx with long pikes and larger shields, and fostered a martial pride among the citizens. At the Battle of Mantinea in 207 BCE he defeated the Spartan ruler Machanidas, reportedly killing him with his own hand. He later fought Nabis of Sparta, and after Nabis was murdered in 192 BCE he brought Sparta into the league. The army's final campaign, in 146 BCE, ended in disaster: Critolaus was defeated by Quintus Caecilius Metellus at Scarpheia in Locris, and Diaeus by Lucius Mummius on the Isthmus, after which Corinth was sacked.

The Achaean League was a true federal state, admired in antiquity and since. Member cities kept their own laws, magistrates and courts, but federal citizenship, foreign policy, war and federal finances belonged to the league. Its chief officer was the general (strategos), elected annually, who commanded the army and presided over the assemblies; he could not hold office in consecutive years, so leaders such as Aratus, general seventeen times by Plutarch's count, served in alternate years. He was assisted by ten damiourgoi, a hipparch, a secretary and a federal council. Regular assemblies (synodoi) met several times a year, at first at Aigion; their exact composition is debated, but they involved the council and citizens over thirty, while extraordinary assemblies (synkletoi), open to all citizens and voting by city, were summoned to decide on war and alliances. Around 188 BCE Philopoemen had the meetings rotated among the member cities. The league arbitrated disputes between members and sent and received embassies as a single state. Its weakness was that larger members, especially Sparta and Messene, had joined unwillingly and repeatedly sought to secede, giving outsiders, first Macedon and later Rome, an opening to intervene in federal affairs.
Roman writers repeated a legend that Lusitanian mares could conceive from the west wind, which was said to explain the remarkable speed of their foals.

The Saxons left a double legacy, in Britain and in Germany. Saxon settlers, with Angles and Jutes, founded the kingdoms of the Anglo-Saxons, and the names Essex, Sussex and Wessex preserve the East, South and West Saxons. Old English and Old Saxon were closely related languages, and the Anglo-Saxons remembered their continental kin: English missionaries went to convert the Old Saxons, among them the two Hewalds, martyred in the 690s, and Lebuin in the 8th century. On the continent Saxony, once conquered, became one of the great regions of the Frankish and German world. The Old Saxon epic Heliand, written around 830, retold the life of Christ in Saxon alliterative verse, presenting Christ as a lord and the disciples as his retainers. The Duchy of Saxony, ruled by the Liudolfing family, produced the kings of East Francia from 919, beginning with Henry the Fowler, and his son Otto I was crowned emperor in 962. The name Saxony later moved east with the ducal title and survives in the German states of Saxony, Lower Saxony and Saxony-Anhalt. In Finnish and Estonian, Germany is still called Saksa and Saksamaa, after the Saxons.

Gwynedd became the leading Welsh kingdom and, under its last princes, the core of an attempt to unite Wales as a single principality. The line of Rhodri the Great, through his sons and his grandson Hywel Dda, supplied kings to much of Wales, and the later dynasties of Deheubarth and Gwynedd both descended from him. The kingdom’s early Christian culture left monuments such as the stone at Llangadwaladr on Anglesey commemorating Cadfan ap Iago as the ‘wisest and most renowned of all kings’. From the twelfth century the princes’ courts sustained the Poets of the Princes, the Gogynfeirdd, among them Meilyr Brydydd, Gwalchmai ap Meilyr and Llywarch ap Llywelyn, known as Prydydd y Moch, whose elaborate praise poetry is a major body of medieval Welsh literature, and the life of Gruffudd ap Cynan, written in Latin and preserved also in Welsh, is a rare secular biography of a Welsh king. The idea of a principality of Wales outlived its creators: Edward I kept the title and gave it to his son Edward of Caernarfon in 1301, and it has been held by heirs to the English and British throne since. Edward’s castles at Caernarfon, Conwy, Harlech and Beaumaris now form a World Heritage Site. North-west Wales remains the region where Welsh is most widely spoken, and the modern county of Gwynedd revives the old name.

Bavaria's influence was greatest along the Danube and in the eastern Alps. Bavarian settlers and the church of Salzburg, raised to an archbishopric in 798, carried Christianity and German speech into Carantania and the lands that became Austria, which began as a Bavarian frontier march under the Babenbergs in 976 and was made a separate duchy only by the Privilegium Minus of 1156. The Bavarian dialects spoken today in Austria and South Tyrol reflect this expansion. Bavarian scriptoria preserved important early texts, among them the Freising manuscripts of around 1000, the oldest surviving writing in a Slavic language in the Latin alphabet, and the Nibelungenlied was probably composed in the Danube region around 1200. Louis IV, the first Wittelsbach emperor, opposed the papacy and sheltered critics such as William of Ockham and Marsilius of Padua at his court in Munich. In the 16th century the Munich court of Albert V employed the composer Orlande de Lassus and built collections that grew into the Bavarian State Library. By championing Catholic reform and leading the Catholic League, the dukes made Bavaria the principal Catholic power of the Empire after the Habsburgs, a role that shaped the course of the Thirty Years' War.

Northumbria was a land of upland pasture and lowland farming, organised in large estates, or shires, that supplied food renders to the king and his nobles. Royal centres such as Bamburgh, Yeavering, where excavations revealed a great timber hall and assembly structure, and later York formed the hubs of power. York, the old Roman city of Eboracum, became the seat of a bishop in 627 and of an archbishop from 735, and its trading quarter developed into a port with links to Frisia and the Rhineland. Christianity came from two directions: Roman missionaries under Paulinus converted Edwin's court, while Oswald brought monks from Iona under Aidan, who founded Lindisfarne in 635. Monasteries became the richest institutions of the kingdom. Benedict Biscop founded Wearmouth in 674 and Jarrow in the early 680s, with books, glaziers and masons brought from Gaul and Rome, and Abbess Hild ruled the double monastery at Whitby. These houses held large endowments of land and produced manuscripts on an extraordinary scale; the Codex Amiatinus alone required the skins of hundreds of calves. Kings issued silver coins from around 700, and in the 9th century small base-metal coins known as stycas circulated in large numbers.

The First Bulgarian Empire's greatest legacy is Slavonic Christian literacy. When disciples of Cyril and Methodius, among them Clement and Naum, were expelled from Moravia in 885–886, Boris I received them and gave them the means to teach. Clement worked at Ohrid in the southwest, while at Preslav scholars developed the Cyrillic alphabet, based on Greek letters, alongside the older Glagolitic script created by Cyril. Simeon I's reign brought a golden age of Slavonic letters: John the Exarch, Constantine of Preslav and Chernorizets Hrabar, author of the treatise On the Letters, translated and composed theological, historical and scientific works. These texts and the Cyrillic script passed to Serbia and to Kievan Rus' after its conversion in 988, and Old Church Slavonic became the liturgical and literary language of much of the Orthodox Slavic world; Cyrillic is today used for Bulgarian, Serbian, Russian, Ukrainian and many other languages. Bulgaria also served as a model of a Christian Slavic monarchy modelled on Byzantium, with its own patriarch and tsar. The Bogomil movement influenced dualist heresies as far west as the Cathars of southern France. The memory of the empire inspired the founders of the Second Bulgarian Empire in 1185 and modern Bulgarian national identity.

The First Bulgarian Empire was the first lasting independent state established on former imperial land in the Balkans, a rival of Byzantium for three centuries, and the cradle of Slavonic Christian literature and the Cyrillic alphabet, which through its schools at Preslav and Ohrid spread across the Orthodox Slavic world.
Boris I's conversion in 864 and the schools of Preslav and Ohrid made it the cradle of Slavonic letters and Cyrillic.

The Kingdom of Asturias did not fall to an enemy; it was transformed by its own success. As Alfonso III pushed the frontier to the Douro, the political centre of the kingdom moved south from the mountains to the plains of León, which offered more land, better communications and a base close to the frontier. In 910 Alfonso III was forced to give up power by his sons, apparently with the support of leading nobles and of his wife, Queen Jimena; he died the same year at Zamora. The realm was divided among his sons: García I took León, the new centre of royal power, Ordoño II took Galicia, and Fruela II took Asturias itself. García died in 914 and Ordoño II succeeded him in León, keeping Galicia, so that León became the principal kingdom and Oviedo a provincial seat. When Ordoño II died in 924, Fruela II succeeded him as king of León, reuniting the inheritance under the crown of León. From this point historians speak of the Kingdom of León as the successor of Asturias. Oviedo remained an important religious centre, with its cathedral and royal pantheon, and Asturias kept its identity as the cradle of the Christian monarchy, but the kingdom itself had ceased to exist as a separate state.
The first Christian kingdom in Iberia after the Muslim conquest, born at Covadonga and seen as the cradle of the Reconquista.

The Emirate of Córdoba made al-Andalus an independent Islamic state with its own dynasty and capital, separate from the Abbasid Caliphate, and laid the foundations for the brilliant Caliphate of Córdoba in the tenth century. Its most famous monument, the Great Mosque of Córdoba, was begun by Abd al-Rahman I around 785 and enlarged by Abd al-Rahman II and later rulers; its forest of columns and double arches of alternating red brick and white stone became a model for Islamic architecture in the western Mediterranean. The emirate brought Eastern culture to the West. The musician Ziryab, who arrived from Iraq in 822, is credited by later tradition with introducing new fashions in music, dress, cuisine and manners at Córdoba, and the polymath Abbas ibn Firnas experimented with glass-making and, reportedly, with flight. The Maliki school of law, established in this period, has dominated Islamic jurisprudence in North-West Africa ever since. The Arabisation of the Christian population created a distinctive Mozarabic culture whose emigrants carried Andalusi styles into the northern Christian kingdoms. The movement of the Martyrs of Córdoba, in which some fifty Christians, including Eulogius of Córdoba, were executed between 850 and 859 for insulting Islam or apostasy, remains one of the best-documented episodes of religious conflict in medieval Spain.

Scottish kings ruled through a small, personal government rather than a large bureaucracy. David I (1124–1153) laid the foundations of the medieval state, developing sheriffdoms, founding royal burghs, issuing the first Scottish coinage and organising the church into territorial dioceses and parishes. The crown passed within the royal house, but repeated royal minorities in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries left regents and noble factions to govern, and several kings met violent ends, among them James I, murdered in 1437. The Parliament of Scotland, a single chamber of the estates of clergy, nobility and burgh commissioners, developed from the thirteenth century; much of its business was prepared by a committee, the Lords of the Articles. Scots law drew on Roman and canon law as well as native custom, and in 1532 James V founded the College of Justice, whose Court of Session remains Scotland’s supreme civil court. In the localities great magnates held hereditary jurisdictions, and in the Highlands clan chiefs ruled with considerable independence. The Reformation of 1560 created a national Kirk governed, after a long conflict over bishops, by Presbyterian courts of kirk sessions, presbyteries, synods and a General Assembly. After the Union of the Crowns in 1603, James VI governed Scotland from London through the Privy Council in Edinburgh, boasting that he ruled it with his pen.

The Saxons of northern Germany, between the Rhine and the Elbe, were conquered by Charlemagne in a series of brutal wars between 772 and 804, during which the Saxon leader Widukind submitted and was baptised in 785. Saxony was then governed by Frankish counts and bishops, and Christianity was spread through new sees such as Paderborn, Bremen and Hildesheim. In the mid-ninth century one Saxon noble family rose above the others. Its founder, Count Liudolf, who died in 866, held lands in eastern Saxony and is described in some sources as dux; with his wife Oda he founded the convent of Gandersheim in 852, which became the family’s religious centre, and his daughter Liutgard married the Carolingian king Louis the Younger. His son Bruno led the Saxons against the Vikings and was killed fighting them in 880, and his younger son Otto the Illustrious held a dominant position in Saxony and Thuringia until his death in 912. Historians debate when the Liudolfings became dukes in a formal sense; their power grew from the defence of East Francia against Vikings, Slavs and Magyars. Otto’s son Henry succeeded him in 912 and in 919 was elected king of East Francia, beginning more than a century of Saxon kingship.

Flanders became one of the most densely populated and urbanised regions of medieval Europe. Land reclaimed from the sea and the coastal marshes supported large flocks of sheep, and from the eleventh century the towns of Ghent, Bruges, Ypres, Arras, Douai and Lille specialised in high-quality woollen cloth, increasingly made from imported English wool. This dependence tied Flanders economically to England, while politically it owed allegiance to France. Ghent, with perhaps 60,000 inhabitants in the fourteenth century, was one of the largest cities north of the Alps. Bruges, linked to the sea by the Zwin inlet and its outport of Damme, became the leading commercial centre of northern Europe, where Italian bankers, Hanseatic merchants and traders from Castile, England and Scotland met; the Hanseatic League kept a kontor there, and the square before the house of the Van der Beurse family gave the word bourse to the language of finance. Cloth workers organised in guilds formed a large urban workforce whose wages and politics often brought violent conflict with the patrician elite. In the late fourteenth and fifteenth centuries the Flemish cloth industry declined under English competition, and the silting of the Zwin moved trade to Antwerp, but Flanders turned to lighter cloths, linen and tapestry and remained one of the richest regions of Europe.
Cîteaux, founded near Dijon in 1098, made Burgundy the cradle of the Cistercian order and of famous monastic vineyards.

Late Anglo-Saxon England was already a remarkably centralised kingdom. It was divided into shires and hundreds, run by ealdormen and royal reeves who became sheriffs; the king issued written writs in English, consulted the witan, or council of leading men, and after Edgar’s coinage reform of about 973 controlled a uniform silver coinage struck at dozens of mints. The Norman kings preserved these structures and added feudal tenure and the Exchequer, which audited sheriffs’ accounts by the early twelfth century. Henry II (r. 1154–1189) developed the common law, with itinerant royal justices, standard writs and sworn juries, and in 1215 rebellious barons forced King John to accept Magna Carta at Runnymede, establishing that the king was bound by law. Parliament grew out of the great council: Simon de Montfort’s assembly of 1265 included knights and burgesses, and by the fourteenth century the Commons sat separately and their consent was needed for taxation. Henry VIII’s break with Rome, enacted through Parliament with the Act of Supremacy of 1534 and directed by Thomas Cromwell, made the king head of the English Church and extended the reach of the state. Conflict between the Stuart kings and Parliament led to civil war, the execution of Charles I and a republic, and the Glorious Revolution of 1688 and the Bill of Rights of 1689 confirmed parliamentary supremacy.

The Caliphate of Córdoba made al-Andalus the wealthiest and most cultured state of tenth-century western Europe, rivalling the Abbasids and Fatimids, and its mosque, palaces, libraries and science left an enduring legacy, even though its sudden collapse in civil war after 1009 broke Muslim Iberia into rival taifa kingdoms.

The Kingdom of Arles left a fainter mark on later history than most medieval kingdoms, but its existence shaped the map of western Europe. Because it belonged to the Holy Roman Empire, the lands between the Rhône, the Saône and the Alps remained for centuries outside the Kingdom of France, and their gradual absorption by France, from Lyon in 1312 and the Dauphiné in 1349 to Provence in 1481, was one of the long processes of French state-building. The weakness of royal power allowed new political units to grow within it: the County of Provence, the Dauphiné of Viennois, the Free County of Burgundy, the County of Savoy, which became a major Alpine state and later gave Italy its royal dynasty, and the cities and bishoprics of western Switzerland, whose lands later joined the Swiss Confederation. The marriage of Conrad’s sister Adelaide to Otto I linked Burgundian lands to the Ottonian imperial project, and the kingdom’s incorporation in 1032 made the emperors rulers of a realm whose title, King of Arles, survived long after any real authority had gone. The region was also a cradle of the Peace and Truce of God, proclaimed in Provence and Burgundy in the early eleventh century, and Provence later became, through its troubadours and the Avignon papacy, a major centre of medieval culture.

Viking-age Danish power rested on fleets and royal fortresses, and Sweyn Forkbeard and Cnut raised the armies that extracted Danegeld from England. Under Valdemar I the Great and Bishop Absalon, Danish fleets fought the Wendish pirates of the southern Baltic and in 1168 took Arkona on Rügen, destroying the temple of Svantevit. Valdemar II “the Victorious” led a crusade to Estonia, where, according to a legend first recorded in the sixteenth century, the Dannebrog flag fell from heaven during the Battle of Lyndanisse in 1219. His capture by Count Henry of Schwerin in 1223 and defeat at the Battle of Bornhöved in 1227 ended Danish dominance over northern Germany. Valdemar IV Atterdag sacked Visby on Gotland in 1361 but lost the ensuing war with the Hanseatic League, ended by the Treaty of Stralsund in 1370.

Denmark–Norway later fought Sweden repeatedly for the Baltic. Christian IV won the Kalmar War of 1611–1613 but was beaten by Tilly at the Battle of Lutter am Barenberge in 1626 during the Thirty Years’ War, and the Torstenson War ended in the losses of the Treaty of Brömsebro in 1645. In 1658 Charles X Gustav of Sweden marched his army across the frozen belts. The navy remained formidable until the British attacked it at the Battle of Copenhagen in 1801 and seized it in 1807. Defeat at Dybbøl in 1864 ended its military ambitions.

Lorraine’s most lasting legacy is dynastic. Francis Stephen, the last duke of the house, married Maria Theresa of Austria in 1736 and became Emperor Francis I in 1745; their descendants, the house of Habsburg-Lorraine, ruled Austria until 1918 and Tuscany until 1859. The Cross of Lorraine, adopted by René II, later became the emblem of the Free French under Charles de Gaulle. The Guise branch shaped the history of France and Scotland. The duchy was also a remarkable artistic centre. The printmaker Jacques Callot of Nancy recorded the horrors of the Thirty Years’ War in The Miseries and Misfortunes of War (1633), Georges de La Tour worked at Lunéville, and the landscape painter Claude Lorrain, born at Chamagne, took his name from his homeland. Joan of Arc came from Domrémy on the borders of Lorraine and Champagne and visited Duke Charles II at Nancy in 1429. Under Stanisław Leszczyński the architect Emmanuel Héré and the ironworker Jean Lamour created the Place Royale, now Place Stanislas, in 1752–1755, one of the finest urban ensembles of eighteenth-century Europe. The duchy’s position between France and Germany foreshadowed the later contest over Alsace-Lorraine.

The principality straddled a language frontier: most of its people spoke Walloon, a dialect of French, but the County of Loon, annexed in 1366, spoke Dutch dialects. The city of Liège grew at the junction of the Meuse and the Ourthe, and the Meuse valley was a corridor of trade between the Rhineland, Champagne and Flanders. Mosan craftsmen were renowned for metalwork: the bronze baptismal font cast by Renier de Huy in the early twelfth century, now in the church of Saint Bartholomew, is a masterpiece of Romanesque art. Coal was mined around Liège from about 1200, among the earliest coal workings in Europe, and fed metalworking, nail-making and later a great arms industry; by the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries Liège and Herstal were among Europe’s largest producers of firearms, selling to armies on all sides. Religious life was intense: the beguine movement had early roots in the diocese, and the visions of Juliana of Cornillon led Bishop Robert of Thourotte to institute the Feast of Corpus Christi in 1246, which Pope Urban IV, a former archdeacon of Liège, extended to the whole church in 1264. The springs of Spa, within the principality, made it a fashionable resort for European aristocrats in the eighteenth century.

Liège was one of the main channels of learning and art in the medieval empire. Notger’s schools trained bishops and scholars for the imperial church, and in the eleventh century Liège was celebrated as a northern Athens. The Mosan school of goldsmiths and metalworkers in the Meuse valley produced works such as the Stavelot Triptych and influenced Romanesque art across Europe, and the brass and copper ware of Dinant gave its name to dinanderie. The Feast of Corpus Christi, first celebrated in Liège, became one of the major festivals of the Catholic church. The composer Johannes Ciconia, born in Liège in the fourteenth century, and the eighteenth-century opera composer André-Ernest-Modeste Grétry carried Liège music abroad, and in 1756 Pierre Rousseau founded the Journal encyclopédique in Liège, an important organ of the French Enlightenment, which later moved to Bouillon. The coal mines and arms workshops made the Liège region one of the first areas of continental Europe to industrialise, and after the principality’s end it became a core of Belgian heavy industry, with the Cockerill works at Seraing occupying the former summer palace of the prince-bishops. The tradition of civic liberty embodied in the Peace of Fexhe and the revolution of 1789 remains part of Walloon identity.

France was the most populous kingdom of Latin Europe: perhaps sixteen to twenty million people around 1300 within its borders of the time, roughly twenty million by 1700 and some twenty-eight million in 1789. The great majority were peasants growing grain, with wine in the Loire valley, Bordeaux and Burgundy, under seigneurs who collected dues and held rights of justice long after serfdom had largely disappeared. Society was described as three orders, clergy, nobility and the third estate, the last including both rich townspeople and the rural poor. In the twelfth and thirteenth centuries the fairs of Champagne linked Flemish cloth makers with Italian merchants, and Paris, with perhaps 200,000 inhabitants around 1300 on some estimates, was the largest city in Latin Christendom. The Black Death from 1348 and the wars that followed cut the population sharply before a long recovery after 1450. The Catholic Church was wealthy and powerful; the Protestant minority, the Huguenots, was tolerated from 1598 but lost that toleration in 1685, when many fled abroad. Under Jean-Baptiste Colbert the crown fostered royal manufactures such as the Gobelins tapestry works and backed projects such as the Canal du Midi, finished in 1681. In the eighteenth century Bordeaux and Nantes grew rich on Atlantic trade in sugar, coffee and enslaved Africans, centred on the colony of Saint-Domingue.

The Árpádian kingdom fixed Hungary's place in Latin Christendom and set institutions that lasted into modern times. Stephen I was canonised in 1083, together with his son Emeric and Bishop Gerard of Csanád, and Ladislaus I in 1192; the dynasty became known for its saints, including Andrew II's daughter Elizabeth of Hungary and Béla IV's daughter Margaret. The Holy Crown, later associated with Stephen though its surviving form dates from the later eleventh and twelfth centuries, became the symbol of the kingdom and of its political community. The Golden Bull of 1222, issued seven years after England's Magna Carta, became a cornerstone of noble liberties and was confirmed by later kings. The union with Croatia in 1102 lasted, in changing forms, until 1918, and the settlement of Germans in Transylvania and the towns shaped the region's ethnic mix for centuries. The kingdom acted as the eastern frontier of Latin Europe, absorbing the Mongol blow of 1241 and settling and converting Cumans and other steppe peoples. Its chronicles, the Gesta Hungarorum written around 1200 by an anonymous notary of a King Béla, probably Béla III, and Simon of Kézai's Gesta of the 1280s, shaped Hungarian historical memory for centuries.

The Duchy of Pomerania was one of the clearest examples of the medieval transformation of the southern Baltic, in which Slavic principalities adopted Christianity, German law and settlement, and urban trade while keeping their native dynasties. Its Christianisation by Otto of Bamberg, later venerated as the Apostle of Pomerania, became a model case of missionary work in the region. Its towns helped make the Hanseatic League the dominant force in Baltic commerce, and their brick Gothic churches and town halls still define the landscape of Stralsund, Greifswald and Szczecin. One Griffin prince, Eric of Pomerania, a great-nephew of Margaret I of Denmark, was crowned king of Denmark, Norway and Sweden in 1397 at the creation of the Kalmar Union; deposed in the late 1430s, he ended his life ruling a small Pomeranian duchy at Darłowo (Rügenwalde). The court culture of the last Griffins is known through objects such as the Croÿ Tapestry of 1554, showing the dynasty with Martin Luther, and the Pomeranian Art Cabinet made in Augsburg for Duke Philip II, together with Eilhard Lubinus’s great map of the duchy of 1618. The division of the duchy in 1648 shaped the borders of Swedish and Brandenburg-Prussian Pomerania for centuries, and the Griffin emblem still appears in regional heraldry in Poland and Germany.

The Norman kingdom is famous for a court culture that drew on Latin, Greek and Arabic traditions. Its monuments, among them the Palatine Chapel with its Byzantine mosaics and Islamic painted ceiling, Cefalù Cathedral and the cathedral of Monreale begun by William II in 1174, are now inscribed together as a World Heritage Site. The Arab geographer al-Idrisi completed his great world geography, the Book of Roger, for Roger II in 1154, and translations of Greek and Arabic works into Latin were made at the court. Frederick II, known as stupor mundi, wrote a treatise on falconry and patronised the Sicilian School of poets, whose love lyrics in a Sicilian vernacular produced the sonnet, usually credited to Giacomo da Lentini, and influenced Dante and Petrarch. The Constitutions of Melfi were one of the most ambitious legal codes of the Middle Ages. The Vespers of 1282 became a symbol of popular resistance and inspired Giuseppe Verdi’s opera, and the division they caused gave rise to two kingdoms both called Sicily and eventually to the name Two Sicilies. Charles V granted Malta, part of the kingdom, to the Knights Hospitaller in 1530. Sicily’s mixed heritage, from Arab-derived place names to Spanish-era Baroque, continues to shape its regional identity within Italy.

Novgorod is the most important example of a republican city-state in medieval Eastern Europe, and its history has often been used, by nineteenth-century liberals and Decembrists as well as later historians, to show that Russian history contained a tradition of self-government before Muscovite autocracy. Because the city was never sacked by the Mongols, it preserved much of early Russian culture. Its churches and icons, the Cathedral of Saint Sophia, the frescoes painted by Theophanes the Greek in the Church of the Transfiguration on Ilyina Street in 1378 and the Novgorod school of icon painting, are among the finest works of medieval Russian art; the historic monuments of Novgorod are a World Heritage Site. The Novgorod First Chronicle is a key source for Russian history, and the birchbark letters have transformed knowledge of everyday life and language in medieval Russia. Novgorod linked Russia to the Baltic and the Hanseatic world, and German merchants’ records of the Peterhof are central sources for Hanseatic trade. Its expansion to the north and east, by colonists, monasteries and fur traders, laid the foundation for the later Russian presence in the European north and beyond the Urals. Its defeats of Swedish and Livonian forces, especially Alexander Nevsky’s victories, entered Russian national memory and were celebrated in Sergei Eisenstein’s 1938 film.

The Crown of Aragon built the first great Iberian empire in the Mediterranean. Through it Sicily from 1282, Sardinia from 1323 and Naples from 1442 came under Iberian rule, which lasted, through the Spanish Monarchy, until the early eighteenth century and shaped the law, administration and aristocracy of southern Italy. Its viceroys, councils and consulates provided models for the later Spanish Empire. The conquests of James I spread the Catalan language and settlers to Valencia and the Balearic Islands, and the Catalan dialect of Alghero in Sardinia survives today. The Crown’s literature and learning were rich: James I left the Llibre dels fets, the chronicles of Bernat Desclot, Ramon Muntaner and Peter IV followed, Ramon Llull wrote widely in Catalan, Arabic and Latin, and Valencia produced the poet Ausiàs March and the novel Tirant lo Blanc, printed in 1490. Gothic buildings such as Palma Cathedral and the Valencia Silk Exchange stand as monuments to its trade. Two popes, Callixtus III and Alexander VI of the Borgia family, came from the Kingdom of Valencia. Its tradition of contractual government and regional law left a lasting mark on Spain, where Aragon, Catalonia, Valencia and the Balearic Islands are separate autonomous communities that share the old royal banner of four red bars on gold.

Moravia's influence was out of proportion to its size. Its name kept alive the memory of Great Moravia and the mission of Cyril and Methodius, central to later Czech and Slovak national histories, and it gave its name to the Moravian Church: Brethren refugees from Moravia settled at Herrnhut in Saxony in 1722 under Count Nikolaus Ludwig von Zinzendorf, and their renewed church sent missionaries to the Caribbean, Greenland, North America and southern Africa. The Kralice Bible served as a model of literary Czech for centuries, and Comenius's writings on education were read across Europe. Moravia's sixteenth-century tolerance, though short-lived, sheltered Anabaptists whose Hutterite descendants live today in North America. In the nineteenth century the land produced a remarkable range of figures. Mendel's work in Brno became a foundation of genetics after its rediscovery in 1900; Tomáš Garrigue Masaryk, first president of Czechoslovakia, was born in Hodonín in 1850 and Sigmund Freud in Příbor in 1856; and the composer Leoš Janáček made his career in Brno. The Austrian Reichstag of 1848–1849 sat at Kroměříž, where it drafted a federal constitution that was never put into force. Moravia's long coexistence of Czech and German speakers, and the Moravian Compromise of 1905, were later discussed as a possible model for managing national conflict within the Habsburg Monarchy.

Brabant was one of the most urbanised regions of medieval Europe. Its four chief towns, Leuven, Brussels, Antwerp and 's-Hertogenbosch, along with smaller centres such as Tienen, Nivelles and Lier, grew rich on woollen cloth woven from English wool, and their guilds and patrician families became both partners and rivals of the dukes. When cloth-making declined in the late fourteenth century the towns turned to luxury trades, and Brussels became famous for tapestries, carved altarpieces and goldsmiths' work. The duchy's commercial centre of gravity then shifted to Antwerp. Its fairs, alongside those of Bergen op Zoom, attracted English cloth merchants, South German financiers such as the Fuggers and, from about 1500, the Portuguese spice trade, and in 1531 the city opened a purpose-built exchange. By the 1560s Antwerp had around 100,000 inhabitants and was the commercial and financial capital of northern Europe, and a centre of printing where Christophe Plantin ran one of the largest presses of the age. Most Brabanters spoke Dutch, but Walloon Brabant around Nivelles spoke French. Religious life was shaped by abbeys such as Villers and Affligem and by mystics including Hadewijch and Jan van Ruusbroec, and the University of Leuven, founded in 1425, became one of the leading universities of Catholic Europe. In the sixteenth century Protestant ideas spread quickly in Antwerp, preparing the conflicts of the Dutch Revolt.

Brabant's influence was political, economic and artistic. The Joyous Entry became one of the best-known charters of liberties in European history: it was invoked against Philip II of Spain during the Dutch Revolt, and the Act of Abjuration of 1581, by which the rebel provinces renounced Philip, is often seen as drawing on its principle that a prince who broke his oath forfeited obedience. Its memory revived in the Brabant Revolution of 1789. Sixteenth-century Antwerp was the first great hub of a world economy linking the Baltic, England, southern Germany, the Mediterranean and the Iberian empires, and its commercial techniques passed to Amsterdam after 1585 along with many of its merchants and craftsmen. Brabant's towns sustained much of the art of the Low Countries: Rogier van der Weyden was city painter of Brussels, Dieric Bouts worked in Leuven, Pieter Bruegel the Elder lived in Antwerp and Brussels, and Peter Paul Rubens made Antwerp the centre of Flemish Baroque painting in the seventeenth century. The University of Leuven trained generations of Catholic scholars, and Erasmus helped to establish its College of the Three Languages in 1517. Brabant's name survives in the Belgian provinces of Flemish Brabant and Walloon Brabant and the Dutch province of North Brabant, the Brussels region lies at the heart of the old duchy, and the Belgian national anthem is called the Brabançonne.

For more than a century and a half after Basil II completed the conquest of the First Bulgarian Empire in 1018, the lands between the Danube and the Balkan Mountains were Byzantine provinces. Discontent grew under the Angelos emperors, and in 1185 an extraordinary tax levied by Isaac II Angelos, linked by the historian Niketas Choniates to the costs of the emperor's wedding to a Hungarian princess, provoked a revolt. Its leaders were two brothers from the region of Tarnovo, Theodore, who took the name Peter, and Asen. Their origins, Bulgarian, Vlach or Cuman, are still debated, and contemporaries described their followers as both Vlachs and Bulgarians. They proclaimed the rising at the dedication of a church of Saint Demetrius in Tarnovo, presenting the warrior saint as having abandoned Byzantine Thessalonica for their cause. Driven north of the Danube in 1186, the brothers returned with Cuman allies and repeatedly defeated Byzantine armies, most notably ambushing Isaac II in the Tryavna pass in 1190. Asen was murdered by boyars in 1196 and Peter in 1197, but their younger brother Kaloyan (r. 1197–1207) secured the new state. He took Varna, negotiated with Pope Innocent III, and in 1204 received a royal crown from a papal legate in return for a nominal union with Rome, winning recognition for the restored monarchy just as the Fourth Crusade broke Byzantine power in Constantinople.

The Second Bulgarian Empire restored Bulgarian statehood, church and letters after almost two centuries of Byzantine rule, and its legacy reached far beyond its borders. The victory at Adrianople in 1205 helped prevent the Latin Empire from consolidating its hold on the Balkans, and Ivan Asen II's alliance with Nicaea strengthened the Greek state that recovered Constantinople in 1261. The restored patriarchate of Tarnovo gave the Bulgarians an autocephalous church of their own. The most lasting impact was cultural. The Tarnovo literary school, associated with Patriarch Euthymius and his disciples, produced saints' lives, liturgical texts and translations in a carefully revised Church Slavonic. After the Ottoman conquest its scholars carried these standards abroad: Gregory Tsamblak worked in Serbia, Moldavia and Lithuania, and Cyprian, probably a Bulgarian by origin, became metropolitan of Kiev and Moscow, so that the Tarnovo reforms spread to Russia in what historians call the second South Slavic influence. In Wallachia and Moldavia, Church Slavonic in its Middle Bulgarian form remained the language of church and chancery for centuries. In Bulgaria the memory of the Asen tsars sustained a sense of nationhood under Ottoman rule; Paisius of Hilendar celebrated them in his Slavonic-Bulgarian History of 1762, and when a Bulgarian state was restored in 1878, Tarnovo hosted the assembly that adopted the Tarnovo Constitution of 1879.

The Second Bulgarian Empire restored Bulgarian independence after nearly two centuries of Byzantine rule, destroyed a Latin crusader army at Adrianople in 1205 and briefly dominated the Balkans under Ivan Asen II, while the Tarnovo literary school it fostered shaped Orthodox Slavic culture from Serbia and Wallachia to Russia.

Jersey preserved a body of Norman customary law and institutions descended from the medieval duchy long after Normandy itself had been absorbed into France, and islanders still toast the monarch as Duke of Normandy. The loyalty of the Carteret family to the Stuarts had a lasting legacy across the Atlantic. Prince Charles found refuge on the island in 1646 and again in 1649–1650, and he was proclaimed king in Saint Helier on 17 February 1649; after the Restoration his brother James, Duke of York, granted Sir George Carteret and Lord Berkeley lands in America that were named New Jersey in 1664. Jersey merchants helped build the cod fisheries of Newfoundland and the Gaspé, Jersey cattle spread around the world as a leading dairy breed, and the island gave its name to the knitted jersey. In the nineteenth century it offered refuge to political exiles, among them Victor Hugo, who lived there from 1852 until his expulsion in 1855, and the actress Lillie Langtry, the Jersey Lily, carried its name into Victorian society. The German occupation of 1940–1945, when the Channel Islands were the only British territory in Europe held by Germany, remains central to island memory. Since the late twentieth century Jersey has become a significant international financial centre, whose low-tax regime has drawn both investment and criticism in debates on offshore finance.
Guild-ruled city-republic on Lake Zürich that joined the Swiss Confederacy in 1351 and became the cradle of Zwingli’s Reformation.

The grand duchy was a land of forest, lakes and rivers where most people farmed rye, kept livestock and paid dues in kind to their lords. Its ethnic and religious make-up changed dramatically with expansion: by the fifteenth century Orthodox East Slavs, ancestors of today's Belarusians and Ukrainians, formed the large majority, while ethnic Lithuanians lived mainly in the north-west. Pagan Lithuanians worshipped deities such as the thunder god Perkūnas and cremated their dead until conversion to Catholicism began in 1387 in Lithuania proper and in 1413–1417 in Samogitia. Vytautas granted privileges to the Jews in 1388 and settled Tatars and Karaites near Trakai, communities whose descendants still live in Lithuania. Furs, wax, honey, timber, potash and later grain flowed down the rivers to Riga, Danzig and Königsberg. In 1557 the Volok Reform of Sigismund II Augustus reorganised royal estates into standard plots, increasing grain output but tightening serfdom. Vilnius, granted Magdeburg rights in 1387, grew into a multi-faith city of Catholic, Orthodox and later Protestant churches and synagogues, and by the eighteenth century it was renowned as a centre of Jewish learning, the home of the scholar known as the Vilna Gaon. Noble landowners, Lithuanian and Ruthenian, came to dominate rural society, while towns remained relatively small and many were owned by magnates.

Reval's most enduring legacy is physical. Because the town escaped large-scale destruction for centuries, its lower town keeps much of its medieval street plan, walls, towers, merchant houses, guildhalls and churches, and the Historic Centre (Old Town) of Tallinn was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1997. Its Gothic town hall, completed in 1404, is often described as the oldest surviving town hall in the Baltic region and Scandinavia, and the spire of St Olaf's Church, rebuilt several times, probably made it one of the tallest buildings in Europe in the sixteenth century. The Lübeck artist Bernt Notke painted the Danse Macabre now displayed in St Nicholas' Church and the altarpiece of the Church of the Holy Spirit, while Hermen Rode's high altar survives in St Nicholas. Reval also served as a vital link in the Hanseatic network, carrying the Russian trade between Novgorod and the West and helping to draw north-eastern Europe into the commercial economy of the Baltic. Its legal and social institutions outlasted its medieval status: Lübeck law, the guilds and the German-speaking urban elite remained dominant in the city's civic life until the early twentieth century, and in 1918 the city became, as Tallinn, the capital of independent Estonia.

The Old Swiss Confederacy showed that peasant and urban communities could defend their liberties against princely power and govern themselves without a king, an example both admired and feared in late medieval Europe. Its infantry transformed warfare: the success of Swiss pikemen against mounted knights helped end the dominance of heavy cavalry, their tactics were copied by the German Landsknechte and by Spain, and Swiss mercenaries served in most major European armies for three centuries. The Confederacy was also a cradle of the Reformation. Huldrych Zwingli began reform in Zürich from 1519, and the allied city of Geneva, where John Calvin worked from 1536 and founded his academy in 1559, became the centre of Reformed Protestantism, whose ideas spread to France, the Netherlands, Scotland, Hungary and the English-speaking world. Basel's printers and scholars made it a hub of humanism. The cantons' avoidance of the Thirty Years' War and later conflicts laid the foundation for Swiss neutrality, recognised internationally in 1815. In the eighteenth century the image of free, virtuous Alpine republics, shaped by writers such as Albrecht von Haller and the Genevan Jean-Jacques Rousseau, influenced European political thought. The Confederacy's institutions, the Landsgemeinde, cantonal sovereignty and consensus through the Diet, remain the historical roots of the federalism and direct democracy of modern Switzerland.

The Angevin kings rebuilt royal power on new foundations. Charles I rewarded loyal barons with offices, castles and their revenues rather than outright grants of land, reformed the coinage and mining royalties, and introduced a household tax, the 'chamber's profit' (lucrum camerae). Louis I's laws of 1351 confirmed the liberties of the Golden Bull of 1222, declared all nobles equal in rights and introduced entail (aviticitas), which kept noble land within families. Under Sigismund (r. 1387–1437), who also became king of Bohemia and Holy Roman Emperor, the royal council and chancery grew, while the leading barons shared power through leagues and the Order of the Dragon, founded in 1408. In the fifteenth century the crown became elective in practice, and the diet, an assembly of prelates, barons, nobles and royal towns, gained the right to elect kings and approve taxes. Matthias Corvinus (r. 1458–1490), elected by the nobility in 1458, centralised government through a professional chancery staffed by lesser nobles and clerics, raised extraordinary taxes nearly every year and reformed the treasury in 1467. Under the Jagiellonian kings Vladislaus II and Louis II the great magnates regained control and royal revenues collapsed, while the lawyer István Werbőczy compiled the customary law of the nobility in the Tripartitum of 1514, which remained the basis of Hungarian noble law until 1848.
Frederick the Wise protected Martin Luther, making Saxony the cradle of the Lutheran Reformation.

Ragusa was the principal intermediary between the Ottoman Balkans and the Christian Mediterranean, and its archive, one of the richest in Europe, is a major source for the economic history of the Balkans from the thirteenth century onwards. It was also a centre of Croatian literature and learning. Renaissance and Baroque writers such as Marin Držić, author of the comedy Dundo Maroje, and Ivan Gundulić, whose epic Osman celebrated the Polish victory over the Ottomans at Khotyn in 1621, made Ragusan Croatian a literary language. The scientist Ruđer Bošković, born in Ragusa in 1711, became one of the leading natural philosophers of the eighteenth century. The republic’s quarantine regulations of 1377, requiring travellers from infected areas to spend a period in isolation outside the city, are often cited as among the earliest such measures in Europe, and its permanent lazaretto outside the walls served as a model. Ragusa’s survival as an independent republic between Venice and the Ottomans for four and a half centuries made it a symbol of liberty for later Croatian national movements. The walled old town of Dubrovnik, with its Renaissance and Baroque palaces, churches and fortifications, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the most visited places in the Mediterranean.

The Crimean Khanate, last great successor of the Golden Horde, was for three centuries the Ottoman Empire’s northern ally and a formidable steppe power whose cavalry raids and slave trade shaped the frontiers of Poland-Lithuania, Muscovy and Ukraine, and it remains the historical state of the Crimean Tatar people.

Denmark-Norway left a lasting imprint on Northern Europe. Its Lutheran church and absolute monarchy shaped the political culture of Denmark and Norway, and the Danish written language became the language of administration and literature in Norway, the basis of the later Bokmål standard. Ludvig Holberg, born in Bergen, wrote comedies and histories that founded modern Danish-Norwegian literature, and the astronomer Tycho Brahe, supported by Frederick II at his observatory of Uraniborg on Hven, made the most precise naked-eye observations of his age; Ole Rømer first measured the speed of light in 1676. The realm also built a modest overseas empire: Tranquebar in India from 1620, forts on the Gold Coast, and St Thomas, St John and St Croix in the West Indies, whose sugar plantations relied on enslaved Africans. The Danish decree of 1792 made Denmark-Norway the first European state to ban the transatlantic slave trade by law. The missionary Hans Egede began the Danish recolonisation of Greenland in 1721, the origin of the present link between Denmark and Greenland. Christian IV’s building projects, including Rosenborg, the Round Tower and the new Norwegian capital of Christiania, founded in 1624, still mark the cities of both countries.

The monarchy was overwhelmingly agrarian. In Bohemia, Moravia and Hungary large noble estates relied increasingly on the forced labour of peasants, the robot, a pattern often called the second serfdom, while the Alpine lands kept a freer peasantry. Mining brought exceptional revenues: silver from Kutná Hora and from Joachimsthal (Jáchymov), whose coins gave the thaler and eventually the dollar its name, mercury from Idrija, copper and gold from the mining towns of Upper Hungary, and salt from the Salzkammergut. Vienna, Prague and later Pest grew as court, administrative and commercial centres, and Charles VI declared Trieste and Fiume free ports in 1719 to open an outlet to the Adriatic. Religion shaped society profoundly. Protestantism spread widely in the sixteenth century, but after 1620 the dynasty enforced Catholicism in Bohemia and Austria, confiscated rebel estates and drove tens of thousands of Protestants into exile, while the Jesuits took over schools and universities. Hungary and Transylvania, by contrast, retained substantial Calvinist and Lutheran communities. The Counter-Reformation produced a pervasive Baroque piety of pilgrimages, monasteries and brotherhoods. In the eighteenth century Maria Theresa’s Urbarium of 1767 regulated Hungarian peasant obligations, and Joseph II abolished personal serfdom in the Bohemian lands in 1781 and in Austria in 1782, though labour dues on the land remained.

The Kingdom of Ireland shaped modern Irish history more than any other period. The plantations, above all in Ulster, created a large Protestant population of English and Scottish origin whose descendants form the core of unionism in Northern Ireland, and the land settlements left a division between landlord and tenant, Protestant and Catholic, that drove Irish politics into the twentieth century. Ulster Presbyterians emigrated in large numbers to the American colonies in the eighteenth century, and the Wild Geese served in the armies of France and Spain. Protestant Ireland produced a remarkable intellectual culture: Trinity College Dublin was founded in 1592, and Jonathan Swift, George Berkeley, Oliver Goldsmith and Edmund Burke were among its writers and thinkers. George Frideric Handel’s Messiah had its first performance in Dublin in 1742, and the Wide Streets Commission of 1757 gave the city its Georgian form. The first printed New Testament in Irish appeared in 1602. Meanwhile Gaelic poetry and learning survived under pressure, recording the destruction of the old order. The radical United Irishmen, founded in 1791 by Theobald Wolfe Tone and others, introduced a non-sectarian republican ideal of Irish independence that later nationalists claimed as their inspiration.

Although a minor state, Parma left a substantial mark on European culture and dynastic politics. The Farnese were among the great art patrons of the age. Their collections, built up by Paul III and his descendants in Rome and Parma, included works by Titian, Raphael and Correggio and the classical sculptures of the Palazzo Farnese in Rome. When Charles of Bourbon left for Naples he took much of this inheritance with him, and it now forms a core of the Capodimonte collections and the National Archaeological Museum in Naples. The Teatro Farnese is an important monument in the history of theatre architecture, one of the earliest theatres built with a permanent proscenium arch. Alessandro Farnese’s campaigns helped fix the frontier between the Spanish Netherlands and the Dutch Republic, roughly the later border of Belgium and the Netherlands. Elisabeth Farnese, as queen of Spain, used her claim to Parma to found Bourbon dynasties in Naples and Parma, reshaping eighteenth-century Italy. The Bodoni press made Parma a centre of fine printing, and Bodoni’s typefaces are still used today. Parma’s musical life, shaped by its ducal theatres, helped nurture the operatic culture of the region, and the Bourbon-Parma family remains a well-known European royal house, related to the grand-ducal family of Luxembourg.
