text: At its height the United Kingdom was the world’s leading industrial, financial and naval power and the centre of the largest empire in history, which by the early 1920s covered about a quarter of the world’s land surface. It spread railways, steam shipping, the telegraph and industrial technology across the globe, and its free-trade policy and the gold standard shaped the nineteenth-century world economy. After abolishing the slave trade in 1807 and, through the Slavery Abolition Act of 1833, slavery in most of its colonies, it pressed other states to end the trade. Its parliamentary institutions and common law were adopted, with variations, in Canada, Australia, New Zealand and other dominions, and English spread as a global language. Science and thought flourished: Charles Darwin’s On the Origin of Species (1859), the work of Michael Faraday and James Clerk Maxwell on electromagnetism, and the economics of David Ricardo and John Stuart Mill. Writers including Jane Austen, Charles Dickens, the Brontë sisters, George Eliot, W.B. Yeats and James Joyce made the period a high point of literature in English. The union with Ireland also left a darker legacy: the Famine and mass emigration created large Irish communities in the United States, Britain and Australia, and the unresolved Irish question shaped politics in both islands throughout the twentieth century.

Bavaria's most lasting legacy is cultural. Ludwig I set out to make Munich a capital of the arts. His architects Leo von Klenze and Friedrich von Gärtner laid out the Ludwigstrasse and built the Glyptothek for classical sculpture and the Alte Pinakothek, opened in 1836, one of the first large public picture galleries in Europe, while the Walhalla near Regensburg, completed in 1842, celebrated German national heroes. He moved the university from Landshut to Munich in 1826. His son Otto became the first King of Greece in 1832, carrying Bavarian officials and classical taste to Athens. Maximilian II invited scholars from northern Germany and founded the Historical Commission in 1858 under the historian Leopold von Ranke. Ludwig II made Munich the scene of Richard Wagner's Tristan und Isolde in 1865 and helped finance the festival theatre at Bayreuth, and his castles of Neuschwanstein, Linderhof and Herrenchiemsee became some of the most visited sights in Europe. Around 1900 Munich was a leading art city: the Munich Secession was founded in 1892, the magazine Jugend gave its name to German Art Nouveau, and the Blue Rider group of Wassily Kandinsky and Franz Marc formed there in 1911. Politically, Bavaria's insistence on its own rights within the empire helped fix the federal character of modern German government.

Luxembourg shows how a small fortress state, created by the great powers in 1815 and partitioned in 1839, turned its steel industry, its neutrality’s failure in two world wars and its position between France and Germany into a central role in European integration and global finance.

The Confederation covered a society that was still largely rural, with serfdom and seigneurial dues being dismantled at different speeds from state to state, and with a population that grew from roughly 30 million to well over 40 million by the 1860s. Religion divided it between a Catholic south and west and a Protestant north and east, and confessional politics remained important in every member state. The league itself had almost no economic powers, and its members kept their own currencies, tolls and weights. Economic integration came instead through the Zollverein, the customs union founded under Prussian leadership on 1 January 1834, which excluded Austria and gradually drew in most of the other states. Railways spread rapidly after the line from Nuremberg to Fürth opened in 1835 and the Leipzig–Dresden line followed in 1839, and the Rhineland, the Ruhr, Saxony and Silesia began to industrialise. Rural poverty, the potato failures and the hunger crisis of 1846–47, and the plight of the Silesian weavers, whose revolt was crushed in 1844, drove emigration, above all to the United States. The period was also one of extraordinary cultural achievement in philosophy, music, scholarship and the universities, though this owed little to the federal institutions themselves.

Belgium, created by revolution in 1830 and guaranteed as neutral by the great powers, became continental Europe’s first industrial nation, ruled the Congo through one of the most notorious colonial regimes, endured two German occupations and turned its divisions between Dutch and French speakers into a federal state at the heart of the European Union.

The Kingdom of Greece was the first new nation state carved out of the Ottoman Empire, and its creation by the intervention and guarantee of the great powers set a pattern followed by Serbia, Romania and Bulgaria. Its pursuit of the Great Idea, and that of its Balkan neighbours, shaped the wars that ended Ottoman rule in Europe, and its territory grew from the narrow state of 1832 to include the Ionian Islands (1864), Thessaly and Arta (1881), Macedonia, Epirus, Crete and the eastern Aegean islands (1912–13), Western Thrace (1920) and the Dodecanese (1947). The defeat of 1922 and the exchange of populations agreed with Turkey at Lausanne in 1923, which brought over a million Orthodox Christians to Greece and sent some 400,000 Muslims to Turkey, ended some three thousand years of Greek life in Asia Minor and became a model, much debated since, for compulsory population transfers. The kingdom fostered a modern Greek culture, with the University of Athens founded in 1837, the long ‘language question’ between the learned katharevousa and spoken demotic Greek, and writers such as Kostis Palamas, Nikos Kazantzakis and the Nobel laureate George Seferis. Athens hosted the first modern Olympic Games in 1896. In the Cold War the Greek Civil War and the Truman Doctrine of 1947 made Greece an early front of American containment policy.

Lithuania’s influence has been greatest at moments of crisis. Its restoration of independence on 11 March 1990, the first by a Soviet republic, challenged the Soviet Union directly and encouraged independence movements in the other republics; the peaceful resistance of January 1991 and the Baltic Way of 23 August 1989, a human chain of some two million people across Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia, became symbols of non-violent struggle. The country’s insistence on legal continuity with the interwar republic helped establish the principle that Soviet annexation had been illegal. The interwar state left a cultural legacy in the modernist architecture of Kaunas, inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2023, in Lithuanian-language schools and scholarship, and in a national passion for basketball that began with victories in the European championships of 1937 and 1939. The trans-Atlantic flight of Steponas Darius and Stasys Girėnas in 1933, which ended in a fatal crash in Germany, became a national legend. The Holocaust in Lithuania, in which around 90 per cent of Lithuania’s Jews were murdered, often with the participation of local collaborators, destroyed the Jewish community of Vilnius, once known as the Jerusalem of Lithuania, and remains a painful subject in public memory.

Communist rule in Czechoslovakia ended suddenly. After the crushing of the Prague Spring, Gustáv Husák presided over two decades of 'normalisation', with purges, censorship and economic stagnation. When the police broke up a student march in Prague on 17 November 1989, mass demonstrations and a general strike followed, organised by Civic Forum in the Czech lands and Public Against Violence in Slovakia. Within weeks the party gave up its leading role, and on 29 December 1989 Václav Havel was elected president, with Dubček as chairman of the Federal Assembly. Free elections followed in June 1990. Yet the end of communism exposed old Czech-Slovak differences, visible in the 'hyphen war' over the state's name, settled in April 1990 as the Czech and Slovak Federative Republic. Slovak politicians wanted looser ties and a gentler economic transition than the rapid market reforms and voucher privatisation favoured in Prague. The June 1992 elections were won by Václav Klaus in the Czech lands and Vladimír Mečiar in Slovakia, who agreed to separate. Slovakia declared sovereignty in July, Havel resigned, and the Federal Assembly voted in November to dissolve the federation. Czechoslovakia ceased to exist on 31 December 1992, succeeded on 1 January 1993 by the Czech Republic and Slovakia.

The Soviet Union was formally a federation of union republics, fifteen from 1956, with autonomous republics and regions for smaller nationalities, and a parliament, the Supreme Soviet, elected without real choice. Real power lay with the Communist Party of the Soviet Union, whose Politburo and General Secretary directed state, economy and society; the party's leading role was written into the 1977 constitution. Its system of appointments, the nomenklatura, controlled careers at every level. The political police, successively the Cheka, OGPU, NKVD and from 1954 the KGB, enforced conformity. Under Stalin, who dominated from the late 1920s until his death in March 1953, terror reached its height: in 1937–1938 alone about 680,000 people were executed. Nikita Khrushchev denounced Stalin's crimes in his secret speech of 1956, presided over the release of most political prisoners from the Gulag and attempted reforms, but was removed in 1964. Leonid Brezhnev's long rule until 1982 brought stability, privilege for officials and growing corruption. Nationality policy fluctuated between the promotion of local languages and elites in the 1920s, deportations of whole peoples such as the Chechens and Crimean Tatars in the 1940s, and Russification later. Gorbachev's reforms after 1985 introduced contested elections and ended the party's constitutional monopoly in 1990.

The Soviet Union was the first state built on Marxist-Leninist ideology and served as a model, patron and rival for communist movements worldwide. Its victory over Nazi Germany, at enormous cost, decided the war in Europe and brought Soviet power into the heart of the continent; communist regimes were installed across Eastern Europe, and the division of Europe and Germany defined the Cold War. The Soviet Union supported revolutionary and anti-colonial movements in China, Korea, Vietnam, Cuba, Angola and elsewhere, and the rivalry with the United States shaped international politics for over four decades, including the Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962. Its achievements in science and technology were real: it launched the first artificial satellite, Sputnik 1, in October 1957 and the first man in space, Yuri Gagarin, on 12 April 1961. Soviet culture combined official socialist realism with world-class achievement in music, ballet, film and literature, from Sergei Prokofiev, Dmitri Shostakovich and Sergei Eisenstein to Boris Pasternak and Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn, whose account of the Gulag shaped Western views of the system. Its legacy still shapes the fifteen successor states, their borders, their large Russian-speaking communities and their conflicts.

Nazi Germany caused the most destructive war in history and the Holocaust. In occupied Europe, mobile killing units of the Einsatzgruppen shot Jews in the Soviet territories from 1941, and the Wannsee Conference of January 1942 coordinated the deportation of Jews from across the continent to extermination camps in occupied Poland: Chełmno, Bełżec, Sobibór, Treblinka, Majdanek and Auschwitz-Birkenau. About six million Jews were murdered, together with hundreds of thousands of Roma, some three million Soviet prisoners of war who died of starvation and abuse, and millions of Polish and Soviet civilians. The Second World War in Europe killed tens of millions. The response to these crimes shaped the post-war order: the Nuremberg trials established that leaders could be judged for aggressive war, war crimes and crimes against humanity, and the Genocide Convention of 1948 and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights followed. The war left Germany divided, moved Poland’s borders westwards and led to the expulsion of some twelve million Germans from eastern Europe. It brought Soviet power into central Europe and set the stage for the Cold War. In Germany the confrontation with the Nazi past became a lasting theme of politics, law, education and memory, and Nazi symbols remain banned there.

Uruk, called Unug in Sumerian, Erech in the Hebrew Bible and Warka today, lay on a branch of the Euphrates in southern Iraq. It grew from two settlements of the Ubaid period, Kullaba and Eanna, which merged during the fourth millennium BCE into a single city. Growth was so rapid that archaeologists named a whole era after it: in the Uruk period, c. 4000–3100 BCE, the city became the largest settlement in the world, covering perhaps 250 hectares by the late fourth millennium, with a population often estimated at 20,000 to 40,000 and possibly more. Its rise rested on irrigated barley farming, date palms, herding and fishing in the marshes, and on two great religious precincts: Eanna, the house of the goddess Inanna, and the terrace of the sky god An in Kullaba, crowned by the whitewashed White Temple. In the Late Uruk phase, c. 3300–3100 BCE, the monumental buildings of Eanna were rebuilt again and again on an unprecedented scale. In the early third millennium the city was enclosed by a wall about 9 kilometres long, which later tradition credited to Gilgamesh. By then Uruk had become one of a number of competing Sumerian city-states, each ruled by its own king and protected by its own god.

Ebla’s rise brought it into conflict with Mari, its chief rival for control of the routes between Syria and Mesopotamia. Texts from the archive, including a long letter from Enna-Dagan of Mari, record campaigns in which Mari’s kings, among them Iblul-Il, conquered towns in Ebla’s sphere, and for a time Ebla delivered large payments of silver and gold to Mari. In the last decades of the archive Ebla turned the tables: in alliance with Nagar and Kish it defeated Mari in a battle apparently fought near Terqa on the Euphrates, an event recorded in the tablets. Ebla’s armies were raised from its towns and villages and led by the king and senior officials, but the texts say little about their organisation. The palace was destroyed by fire around 2300 BCE. Sargon of Akkad listed Ebla among lands given to him by the god Dagan, and Naram-Sin later boasted of conquering Ebla, so either may have been responsible, though some scholars argue that Mari took revenge first. In the second millennium the rebuilt city was protected by massive earthen ramparts with stone-built gates, enclosing an area of about 56 hectares. These defences could not save it from a Hittite attack around 1600 BCE, probably by Mursili I or his predecessor Hattusili I.
Zimri-Lim boasted of building an ice house at Terqa, a feat he said no earlier king had achieved, to keep ice for cooling drinks at court.

Dilmun is named in Mesopotamian texts long before it can be located with certainty. Archaic tablets from Uruk of the late fourth millennium BCE already mention it, and Ur-Nanshe of Lagash (c. 2500 BCE) recorded that the ships of Dilmun brought him timber from foreign lands. Sargon of Akkad later boasted that ships from Dilmun, Magan and Meluhha moored at the quay of his capital Agade. In the third millennium the name probably covered parts of the eastern Arabian coast, including Tarut Island, before it came to centre on the island of Bahrain. Around 2200 BCE the settlement at Qal’at al-Bahrain on the north coast began to grow, and by about 2050 BCE it was a walled town with paved streets, houses and storerooms, the core of what archaeologists call the Early Dilmun or Barbar culture. Temples rose at Barbar and Diraz, and a planned village with its own temple developed at Saar. The island’s great asset was fresh water: artesian springs on land and even beneath the sea made it a natural harbour and watering station on the route between southern Mesopotamia and the copper and stone sources of Magan, in present-day Oman, and the Indus Valley beyond.

Urartu was a land of high plateaus and mountain valleys with long, harsh winters, and its prosperity depended on making the most of short growing seasons. The kings invested heavily in irrigation: Menua’s canal, which carries water for more than 50 kilometres from springs south of Van to the city, is still in use and was long known locally as the canal of Shamiram. Royal inscriptions record the planting of vineyards, orchards and fields alongside the founding of fortresses, and excavated storerooms at Karmir Blur, Ayanis and Bastam held rows of huge clay jars, some marked with their capacity, for wine, grain and oil. Horse breeding was renowned, and the Assyrian account of Sargon II’s campaign of 714 BCE describes the region’s herds and the training of cavalry horses. Urartian metalworkers produced bronze shields, helmets, quivers, belts and large cauldrons decorated with lions, bulls and winged figures. Economic life centred on the king and the fortress centres, which collected and redistributed produce, while most of the population probably lived as farmers and pastoralists in villages. Religion was organised around a state pantheon headed by Haldi, with the storm god Teisheba and the sun god Shivini; the rock niche of Meher Kapısı near Van lists dozens of deities and the sacrifices due to each.

The Kingdom of Iberia, or Kartli, was the cradle of Georgian statehood: it guarded the Caucasus passes between Rome and Persia for nearly nine centuries, became one of the first Christian kingdoms in the 4th century and produced the earliest Georgian script and literature before Persia abolished its monarchy.

Pontus was a hereditary monarchy in which the king stood at the centre of power, surrounded by a court of ‘friends’, relatives and officials in the Hellenistic manner, with Persian elements in its titles and rituals. The dynasty claimed descent from the Achaemenid royal house, and Mithridates VI also boasted descent from Alexander the Great and the Seleucids, presenting himself as heir to both Persian and Macedonian kingship. The interior was governed through royal fortresses and districts under appointed officials, while the Greek cities kept their own councils and magistrates under royal supervision and the great temple states remained semi-autonomous under their priests. The kings used marriage and diplomacy to secure their position: Mithridates II married a Seleucid princess, Mithridates V sent help to Rome in the Third Punic War and against Aristonicus in Asia and was rewarded with Phrygia, which Rome later withdrew, and Mithridates VI married his daughter Cleopatra to Tigranes the Great of Armenia. Mithridates VI himself came to power after a regency of his mother Laodice, whom he imprisoned around 113 BCE. Succession disputes and court intrigue remained frequent, and the kings relied heavily on Greek generals, admirals and advisers to run their wars and their finances.

Pontus mattered most as the base of Mithridates VI, whose wars against Rome lasted, with intervals, from 89 to 63 BCE and shaped the politics of the late Roman Republic. The First Mithridatic War gave Sulla the command and the army that he turned against Rome itself, and the Third made the careers of Lucullus and Pompey; the extraordinary command granted to Pompey under the Lex Manilia in 66 BCE was a milestone in the concentration of power that ended the Republic. Mithridates’ order in 88 BCE to kill the Romans and Italians in Asia, the so-called Asiatic Vespers, in which ancient sources claim that 80,000 or more people died, became notorious, and the welcome he received as a liberator in Greek cities such as Athens showed how resented Roman rule had become. Pompey’s settlement joined western Pontus to Bithynia to form the province of Bithynia et Pontus and gave the rest to client rulers. The king himself became a legend: his supposed immunity to poison, built up by taking small doses, gave the word mithridatism, and the antidote called mithridatium was prescribed in European medicine for centuries. He inspired works from Racine’s Mithridate to Mozart’s opera Mitridate, re di Ponto.

The end of the Albanian kingdom came through the tightening of Sasanian control rather than through a single conquest. In 450–451 Albanians joined the Armenian and Iberian rising against the attempt of the Sasanian king Yazdegerd II to impose Zoroastrianism on the Christian Caucasus, a rising crushed at the Battle of Avarayr in 451. A further revolt by King Vache II around 459 ended with his abdication, and for about a quarter of a century the kingship lapsed while Persian officials governed the country. The Sasanian king Balash restored it around 485 in the person of Vachagan III, a member of the old royal family, as part of a wider settlement with the Christian Caucasus after renewed Armenian resistance. Vachagan's reign was remembered as a golden age of church building and reform. After his death, around 510, the Sasanians abolished the kingship again and governed Albania through marzbans, Persian governors based at Partav. Local rule revived in the early seventh century under the Mihranid family, whose princes navigated between Persia, Byzantium, the Khazars and finally the Arabs. The Arab conquest from the 640s brought Arran, as it was now called, into the caliphate, and the Albanian language and separate church faded over the following centuries.

The Alans were an Iranian-speaking people of the steppes north of the Caucasus and the Caspian, closely related to the Sarmatians and the earlier Scythians. Their name is generally thought to derive from an old Iranian form related to Aryan. They appear in Greek and Latin sources in the first century CE, when Roman writers such as Seneca, Lucan and the Jewish historian Josephus begin to mention them as a new and formidable power between the Don and the Caucasus. Chinese sources of the Han period refer to a people called Yancai, later renamed Alanliao, north-west of the Caspian, which many scholars connect with the rise of the Alans, although the identification is debated. The Alans probably formed as a new confederation within the Sarmatian world, absorbing the Aorsi and other groups and drawing in peoples of different origins. The historian Ammianus Marcellinus, writing in the late fourth century, describes how they had gradually overcome their neighbours and given them their own name, so that 'Alans' covered many peoples spread across the steppe from the Don eastwards. They were never a single state with fixed borders, but a shifting union of clans and chiefdoms bound by language, way of life and military success, whose leaders could combine for great raids and then disperse.

The Buyid dynasty, Daylamite Shia emirs who ruled western Iran and Iraq and controlled the Abbasid caliphs from 945 to 1055, created the model of a secular ruler beside a powerless caliph and presided over a remarkable flowering of Islamic science, philosophy and Shia scholarship.

The kingdom’s age of greatness, from David IV to Tamar, left a deep mark on Georgian identity. It was the period of Shota Rustaveli’s epic The Knight in the Panther’s Skin, written around 1200 and dedicated to Tamar, which became the national poem of Georgia. David IV founded the Gelati monastery near Kutaisi in 1106 with an academy where scholars such as Ioane Petritsi and Arsen Iqaltoeli translated and commented on Greek theology and philosophy. The rock-cut monastery of Vardzia, consecrated in the 1180s, the Bagrati Cathedral at Kutaisi and the rebuilt Svetitskhoveli Cathedral at Mtskheta, finished around 1029, show the ambition of Georgian church architecture, while goldsmiths and fresco painters produced works of high quality. Historians compiled the chronicles later gathered as Kartlis Tskhovreba, the Life of Georgia. Beyond its borders the kingdom dominated Shirvan and much of Armenia, and Tamar helped her kinsmen Alexios and David Komnenos seize Trebizond in 1204, founding the Empire of Trebizond. It sheltered Orthodox institutions from Athos to Jerusalem. Later Georgians looked back to the united kingdom as the model of statehood; David the Builder and Tamar were canonised by the Georgian Orthodox Church and remain central figures of national memory.

The Sultanate of Rum laid the foundations of Turkish Anatolia. Under its rule the peninsula, Greek-speaking and Christian for more than a millennium, began its long transformation into a predominantly Turkish and Muslim land; Western writers were calling it Turchia by the time of the Third Crusade. The Seljuks left a remarkable architectural legacy in carved stone: the Alaeddin Mosque in Konya, the Karatay Madrasa of 1251, the Ince Minareli Madrasa, the Gök Madrasa at Sivas and the network of caravanserais, with their elaborate portals, are among the finest monuments of medieval Islamic architecture. Konya became a centre of Persian literature and Sufism. Rumi, who died there in 1273, wrote the Masnavi, one of the most influential works of Persian poetry, and his followers formed the Mevlevi order of whirling dervishes. Ibn Bibi’s Persian chronicle preserves the history of the dynasty. Politically the sultanate shaped the world that followed it. The Turkish principalities, or beyliks, that emerged from its collapse, including the Karamanids and the Ottomans, inherited its institutions, artistic models and frontier culture, and Ottoman tradition later claimed that the Seljuk sultan had granted Osman’s family their first lands.

For a few decades the Aq Qoyunlu made western Iran and eastern Anatolia the seat of a major power that could challenge both the Ottomans and the Timurids. Their contacts with Venice formed one of the earliest attempts at an alliance between a European state and an Iranian ruler against the Ottomans, and the reports of Venetian envoys such as Ambrogio Contarini are important sources for the region. The confederation’s most lasting legacy was the Safavid state. Shah Ismail I was a grandson of Uzun Hasan through his daughter, and the Safavids took over the Aq Qoyunlu capital at Tabriz, much of their territory, their Turkmen tribal army, which became the core of the Qizilbash, and many of their Persian bureaucrats and administrative practices. In eastern Anatolia the Ottomans kept the Aq Qoyunlu tax regulations in force after their conquest of the region, citing the law of Hasan Padishah in their provincial law codes for Diyarbakır and neighbouring districts. The court of Tabriz was also a centre of Persian culture. The poet Jami dedicated his allegory Salaman and Absal to Ya’qub, and the Turkmen style of manuscript painting developed in Tabriz under Aq Qoyunlu patronage fed directly into the celebrated painting workshops of the early Safavid shahs.

Circassian society was organised by rank and by kinship. In the princely societies, such as Kabarda, Temirgoy, Bzhedugh, Hatuqwai and Besleney, hereditary princes, the pshi, stood above a class of nobles, the work, who served them as warriors and counsellors, and beneath these lived free peasants, dependent peasants and slaves. Among the Shapsugs, Natukhaj and Abadzekhs of the west, the power of princes and nobles was weaker and largely broken in the late eighteenth century, and free communities governed themselves. A strict unwritten code of conduct, Adyghe Khabze, regulated hospitality, honour, respect for elders, and relations between ranks and between men and women. Noble children were often raised by foster families of lower rank, a custom known as atalyk that bound families together. The economy rested on millet and other grains, orchards, beekeeping and above all livestock, and Circassian horses, such as the Kabardian breed, were famous. Trade ran mainly to the Black Sea ports, where Circassians exchanged hides, honey, wax, timber and slaves for salt, textiles and metal goods. Religion changed over the centuries: older beliefs mixed with Christianity in the Middle Ages, and Sunni Islam spread from the sixteenth to the early nineteenth century through Crimean and Ottoman influence, first among the nobility and then more widely.

The Qawasim were the most formidable naval power of the lower Gulf around 1800, and their attacks on shipping, including vessels under British protection, led the British authorities in India to describe them as pirates. Many historians now see their warfare as part of wider commercial and political rivalries in the Gulf, including the conflict between Oman and the Wahhabi movement, with which the Qawasim were then aligned. British expeditions sailed from Bombay in 1809 and again in 1819, when Ras al-Khaimah was taken and Qasimi vessels and forts along the coast were destroyed. The General Maritime Treaty of 1820, signed by Sultan bin Saqr among others, banned piracy and maritime raiding, and a Maritime Truce first concluded in 1835 and made perpetual in 1853 forbade warfare at sea between the rulers. Conflict on land continued: Sharjah fought its neighbours over grazing grounds, towns and the loyalty of tribes, and in 1940 there was a brief war between Sharjah and Dubai. Defence rested on the ruler’s retainers, armed townsmen and allied Bedouin, supported by watchtowers and forts such as the Al Hisn fort in Sharjah town. In 1951 the British formed the Trucial Oman Levies, later the Trucial Oman Scouts, with their headquarters at Sharjah, and the Royal Air Force kept a station at the Sharjah airfield until 1971.

The United Arab Emirates has not declined: it remains a federation of seven emirates under its 1971 constitution and the same ruling families. Its history since independence has been one of consolidation and transformation rather than rupture. Federal institutions gained strength over time, the defence forces were unified and the provisional constitution became permanent in 1996, while Abu Dhabi's wealth increasingly bound the other emirates to the centre. That dependence became clear when Abu Dhabi provided 10 billion dollars to Dubai during the debt crisis of Dubai World in 2009, after which the tower then nearing completion was named Burj Khalifa in honour of the president. The economy has diversified, with non-oil activities now forming most of its output, although hydrocarbons still fund much of the state; the country introduced value added tax in 2018 and a federal corporate tax in 2023, and the Barakah nuclear power plant, the first in the Arab world, began commercial operation in 2021. Its challenges include dependence on foreign labour, criticism of its human rights record, the security risks of its regional interventions, shown by Houthi missile and drone attacks on Abu Dhabi in January 2022, and preparation for a world less dependent on oil. Under Mohamed bin Zayed the UAE stands as one of the most influential smaller powers in the Middle East.

Magadha's strength rested on its land. The middle Ganges plain received ample rainfall, and the spread of wet-rice cultivation, aided by iron tools, produced surpluses that supported a growing population, towns and a large army. The hills to the south supplied iron ore and timber, and their forests sheltered the elephants that became the backbone of Magadhan armies. The period saw what archaeologists call the second urbanisation of India: fortified towns such as Rajagriha, Champa and later Pataliputra grew along rivers and trade routes, the fine Northern Black Polished Ware spread as a luxury pottery, and silver punch-marked coins came into use. Merchants, some of them organised in guilds, traded along the Ganges and the overland routes linking Magadha with Kosala, Kashi and the Deccan. Society was divided by varna and occupation, but Magadha was less bound by Brahmanical orthodoxy than the western Ganges valley, and it became the setting of a remarkable religious ferment. Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha, attained enlightenment at Bodh Gaya in Magadha and preached at Rajagriha, where Bimbisara gave his order the Veluvana bamboo grove; Vardhamana Mahavira, the great teacher of Jainism, also taught in the region, and the Ajivikas of Makkhali Gosala were active there. These movements found many lay supporters among merchants and townspeople.

The Pallava kingdom was an agrarian society centred on the plains of Tondaimandalam and the Kaveri delta, where irrigation tanks, many of them built or endowed by kings and local communities, sustained rice cultivation. Royal charters granted villages to Brahmins as brahmadeya and to temples as devadana, spreading Brahmin settlements and temple estates that became centres of agricultural expansion and learning. Kanchipuram was a great city of temples, monasteries and colleges; the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang, who visited around 640, described its many Buddhist monasteries, its Hindu temples and its numerous Jains. Its ghatika, a college of Brahmin learning, was renowned across the south. The Pallava age saw the decisive rise of devotional Hinduism in the Tamil country: the Shaiva Nayanars, such as Appar and Sambandar, and the Vaishnava Alvars, such as Tirumangai Alvar, composed Tamil hymns that drew worshippers to temples and turned many away from Jainism and Buddhism. Trade flowed through ports such as Mamallapuram to Sri Lanka, Southeast Asia and China, carried by merchant guilds; a Tamil inscription at Takua Pa in southern Thailand, which mentions a tank named after a title of Nandivarman III and a merchant guild, the Manigramam, attests to these links across the Bay of Bengal.

The Pallavas transformed the architecture and art of South India. Under Mahendravarman I the first rock-cut shrines of the Tamil country were excavated, and his Mandagapattu inscription boasts of a temple made without brick, timber, metal or mortar. At Mamallapuram, the port named after Narasimhavarman I, Pallava sculptors carved cave temples, the monolithic shrines known as the Five Rathas and the great relief usually called Arjuna's Penance or the Descent of the Ganges; under Rajasimha came the structural Shore Temple and the Kailasanatha temple at Kanchipuram, followed by the Vaikuntha Perumal temple. These works, at Mamallapuram now a World Heritage Site, laid the foundations of the Dravidian temple style later developed by the Chola Empire. Under Pallava patronage Kanchipuram, counted among the seven sacred cities of Hinduism, flourished as a centre of Sanskrit learning, and the bhakti hymns of the Nayanars and Alvars composed in their age became the scriptures of Tamil Shaivism and Vaishnavism. Beyond India, the Pallava form of the Grantha script, used to write Sanskrit, was adopted in Southeast Asia, where early inscriptions in Cambodia, Champa, Java and the Malay world use scripts derived from it, and Pallava architectural forms influenced early temples in the region.

Little is known of the organisation of Satavahana armies, but inscriptions refer to victorious camps from which kings issued orders, and the realm relied on infantry, cavalry and elephants like other Indian states of the time. Its history was shaped by wars on several fronts. Kharavela of Kalinga claims in his Hathigumpha inscription to have sent an army westward in defiance of Satakarni. The main rivals, however, were the Western Satraps, Saka rulers of Gujarat, Malwa and western India who were probably at first subordinate to the Kushan Empire. In the late first and early second centuries CE the Kshaharata ruler Nahapana occupied much of the western Deccan, including Nashik and the ports of the Konkan, as his family's inscriptions in the local caves show. Gautamiputra Satakarni reversed this in a campaign usually dated to around 125 CE, destroying the Kshaharata dynasty; a large hoard found at Jogaltembi near Nashik contains thousands of Nahapana's silver coins restruck with Gautamiputra's name. The recovery did not last. The Junagadh inscription of Rudradaman I, the Western Satrap ruler of the Kardamaka line, dated 150 CE, boasts that he twice defeated Satakarni, lord of the south, but spared him because of their close relationship, a reference to a marriage alliance between the two houses. Yajna Sri Satakarni later regained some western territory.

The most lasting legacy of the Chalukyas of Badami is architectural. Within two centuries their craftsmen moved from the rock-cut caves of Badami, excavated in the late sixth century, to free-standing stone temples at Aihole, such as the Lad Khan and Durga temples, and then to the mature complex at Pattadakal. There the Virupaksha temple, built around 740 by Queen Lokamahadevi to commemorate Vikramaditya II’s victory over the Pallavas, stands beside temples in the northern Nagara style, making Pattadakal a meeting point of the two great traditions of Indian temple building; the site was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987. Chalukya builders drew on the Pallava Kailasanatha temple at Kanchipuram, and their work in turn shaped the Rashtrakuta dynasty, whose rock-cut Kailasa temple at Ellora is often compared with the Virupaksha. The Aihole inscription of 634, composed by the poet Ravikirti, names the poets Kalidasa and Bharavi and so provides a firm latest date for both. Politically, the dynasty made the Deccan a lasting counterweight to the kingdoms of the Ganges plain and drew the Kannada country into the mainstream of Indian statecraft. Its name outlived it: the Eastern Chalukyas ruled Vengi until the eleventh century, and the Western Chalukyas of Kalyani, who rose in 973, claimed descent from the house of Vatapi.

The empire remained formidable under Krishna III, but its strength depended on his personal leadership and on loyal feudatories. After his death in 967 his brother Khottiga faced the Paramara ruler Siyaka II of Malwa, a former vassal, who invaded the Deccan and sacked Manyakheta in 972, an event recorded by the poet Dhanapala. The blow exposed the weakness of the throne. In 973 Tailapa II, a feudatory based in the Bijapur region who claimed descent from the Chalukyas of Badami, overthrew Khottiga’s nephew Karka II and proclaimed the Western Chalukya Empire, soon making himself master of most of the old Rashtrakuta lands. Resistance continued in the south, where the Western Ganga king Marasimha II and his general Chavundaraya backed Indra IV, a grandson of Krishna III, as Rashtrakuta claimant. The cause collapsed after Marasimha’s death, and Indra IV died in 982 at the Jain centre of Shravanabelagola by the ritual fast of sallekhana, ending the imperial line. Minor Rashtrakuta families persisted as local chiefs, and some later dynasties of northern India claimed descent from them, though these links are uncertain. The Western Chalukyas inherited the empire’s position in the Deccan, continuing its rivalry with the Cholas for another two centuries.
It carved the Kailasa temple at Ellora and fostered the earliest surviving Kannada literature and major Jain scholarship.

The empire covered the black-soil plateau of the Deccan and the fertile valleys of the Krishna and Tungabhadra, where tanks and canals watered rice, sugarcane and cotton alongside dry crops of millet and pulses. Its prosperity rested on agriculture and on the activity of powerful merchant guilds. The best known, the Ainnurruvar or Five Hundred Lords of Ayyavole, based at Aihole, traded across peninsular India and overseas to Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia, and its inscriptions record privileges granted by kings and local lords. Towns such as Lakkundi, Balligave and Kalyani grew as centres of trade, minting and religion. Religious life was plural. Shaiva sects, including the Kalamukha ascetics who ran large temple colleges at Balligave and elsewhere, enjoyed strong royal patronage; Jainism remained influential, especially among merchants and noblewomen such as Attimabbe, who sponsored copies of Ponna’s works and a Jain temple at Lakkundi; and Vaishnavism grew. Brahmin settlements called agraharas and temple mathas served as schools for Sanskrit learning, logic and law. Society was organised by caste and occupation, with village assemblies, landholders and guilds playing an active role in local life, as thousands of Kannada inscriptions on temple walls and stone tablets record gifts, disputes and public works.
The Karnataka dynasty famous for the intricately carved temples of Belur, Halebidu and Somanathapura, and the last great power of the region before Vijayanagara.

Vijayanagara shaped the political and cultural map of southern India for centuries. Its patronage fostered literature in Sanskrit, Kannada, Telugu and Tamil. Under the early Sangama kings the scholar Sayana and his collaborators produced commentaries on the Vedas that became standard. Krishnadevaraya himself composed the Telugu poem Amuktamalyada, and his court is associated with celebrated poets such as Allasani Peddana. The composer Purandara Dasa, traditionally regarded as the father of Carnatic music, lived and worked within the empire. Vijayanagara architecture, with its tall gateway towers, pillared halls carved with horses and mythical beasts and large temple-city complexes, set a style followed across the south, and many temples in Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh were rebuilt or enlarged under its rule. The ruins of the capital at Hampi were inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1986. Politically, the nayaka kingdoms that succeeded it, including Madurai, Thanjavur, Gingee, Ikkeri and the Wodeyars of Mysore, inherited its institutions and claimed its legitimacy. Even foreign trade was affected: in 1639 the English East India Company obtained the site of Madras, where it built Fort St George, from a local nayaka subordinate to the Aravidu kings. In modern times Vijayanagara has been invoked as a symbol of south Indian and Hindu resistance, a reading that historians often treat with caution.
